claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a relatively homogeneous fcc matrix.
Additive processing establishes fine microstructural features in the alloy.
High-temperature degradation is governed by the formation or suppression of a continuous protective oxide layer.
In oxidizing environments, Cr and Ti preferentially oxidize.
Preferential oxidation produces a brittle oxide scale at the surface and along grain boundaries.
The oxide scale concentrates stress and initiates crack propagation.
A Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale is adherent to the underlying alloy.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide scale and fcc matrix generates interfacial stress.
Oxide-induced interfacial stress causes microcrack formation.
Under reducing conditions, a protective oxide layer is absent or suppressed.
The absence of a protective oxide under reducing conditions promotes internal defect accumulation.
Reducing exposure produces oxygen vacancies and voids along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary defects generated under reducing conditions reduce ductility and cause localized failure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a continuous but brittle oxide scale associated with interfacial cracking.
Reducing exposure will produce internal voids or localized embrittlement without a protective surface layer.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will decrease fracture toughness relative to the starting state.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will decrease yield strength relative to the starting state.
Temperatures above approximately 700°C are sufficient to activate the proposed oxidation or reduction processes.
Exposure must persist long enough for oxide-scale formation or internal-defect accumulation.
Changing only the atmosphere between oxidizing and reducing conditions will reveal distinct oxide-scale and internal-defect degradation pathways.
